addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	//! Generic bench driver: the [`Bench`] trait, adaptive outer/inner
2	//! loop sizing, and the band-histogram report.
3	
4	use std::hint::black_box;
5	
6	use hdrhistogram::Histogram;
7	
8	use crate::bands::{self, BandLabels};
9	use crate::dither::Dither;
10	
11	const WARMUP: u64 = 10_000;
12	const ESTIMATE_STEPS: u64 = 1_000;
13	const ESTIMATE_SAMPLES: usize = 5;
14	const FRAMING_DOMINATION_RATIO: f64 = 10.0;
15	const MAX_INNER: u64 = 1_000;
16	
17	/// Timer pairs per *timed group* inside a micro-probe.
18	///
19	/// - The probe's unit of measurement is a group, not a single
20	///   pair: one `Instant` pair brackets [`PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS`]
21	///   pairs and the total is divided down to a per-pair value.
22	/// - **Why group at all:** the timer reads integer nanoseconds,
23	///   so a single ~25 ns pair is quantized to ~4% — coarser than
24	///   the frequency-ramp movement the environment grade exists to
25	///   see (~9% on the 3900X). A 64-pair group totals ~1.6 µs, so
26	///   the same 1 ns quantum is ~0.06% of the value, and the
27	///   per-pair figure lands on a ~15 ps lattice.
28	/// - Grouping costs the *census* its sensitivity, so the census
29	///   is counted per pair instead — see [`Prober::probe`].
30	const PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS: usize = 64;
31	
32	/// Timed groups per micro-probe — the population its floor and
33	/// spread quantiles are taken over.
34	///
35	/// - 128 groups of [`PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS`] is ~8,192 pairs, about
36	///   256 µs. Sized against the batch seam it runs in, which
37	///   already costs 1-2 ms (a `select_nth_unstable` plus 65,536
38	///   histogram records), so a probe adds a fraction of a gap
39	///   that already exists rather than a new one.
40	const PROBE_GROUPS: usize = 128;
41	
42	/// Micro-probes taken during warmup, spread evenly across it —
43	/// the leading stretch of the environment series, and the only
44	/// stretch measured before the bench starts running (see
45	/// [`crate::gauge::EnvGrade`]). The rest of the series is
46	/// sampled at batch seams across the whole run.
47	const WARMUP_PROBES: usize = 16;
48	
49	/// Trailing stretch of warmup (seconds) that the warmup grade
50	/// reads: its tail window.
51	///
52	/// - Warmup's job is to absorb a ramp, so grading the whole
53	///   stretch would fault a warmup that did exactly that. The
54	///   question worth asking is "did it end settled", which is a
55	///   window at the tail.
56	/// - **Time, not probe count.** A count-based window is a
57	///   fraction of however many probes were taken, so
58	///   [`DEFAULT_SETTLE_TIME_S`] of warming made the last-8-of-N
59	///   window warmup's second half, which straddles a ramp
60	///   ending at ~0.8 s and grades it F. A fixed 300 ms asks the
61	///   same question of every run: was the box steady over the
62	///   last 300 ms before measurement started.
63	/// - Short warmup stretches (every bench after the first, ~4 ms
64	///   of [`WARMUP_PROBES`] probes) fall entirely inside the
65	///   window, so the whole stretch is graded, as before.
66	/// - The "Dynamic warmup" Todo turns this window into
67	///   the *exit condition* — warm until the trailing window
68	///   grades A — at which point the grade and the stopping rule
69	///   are one computation.
70	const WARMUP_TAIL_SECONDS: f64 = 0.3;
71	
72	/// Default wall seconds the **first** run in a process spends
73	/// stepping the bench before any samples are recorded: the
74	/// `--settle-time` / `settle_time` default.
75	///
76	/// - **The first bench of every process reports numbers ~8.6%
77	///   slow otherwise.** Measured on a 7600x 2026-07-29: `min-now`
78	///   reads 17.6 ns as the process's first bench against 16.2 ns
79	///   once warm, and its env bench stretch grades `step 11.05% F`
80	///   while benches
81	///   2-17 of the same process grade env-clean. The P-state boost
82	///   is machine state, so every later bench inherits it. The
83	///   warm belongs to the process, not to each run.
84	/// - 1.5 s rather than 1.0: the ramp measured at ~150-200 ms but
85	///   the 3900X's relaxation lands later, and the tail window
86	///   ([`WARMUP_TAIL_SECONDS`]) needs settled time behind it.
87	/// - Cost is ~2% of an `all -d 5` sweep (~85 s to ~86.5 s), paid
88	///   once, against a wrong histogram on whichever bench ran
89	///   first.
90	pub const DEFAULT_SETTLE_TIME_S: f64 = 1.5;
91	
92	/// Wall seconds of stepping between micro-probes during the
93	/// process warm: ~150 probes over [`DEFAULT_SETTLE_TIME_S`], so
94	/// the ~300 ms tail window holds ~30 and the series resolves a
95	/// transition to ~10 ms.
96	const PROCESS_WARM_PROBE_GAP_S: f64 = 0.01;
97	
98	/// Steps between elapsed-time checks during the process warm, so
99	/// a cheap bench doesn't spend the warm inside `Instant::now`.
100	const PROCESS_WARM_STEP_CHUNK: usize = 64;
101	
102	/// Quantile defining a micro-probe's floor, matching
103	/// [`BATCH_FLOOR_Q`]'s reasoning: the left edge is sparse, a
104	/// tenth of the population is not.
105	const ENV_FLOOR_Q: f64 = 0.10;
106	
107	/// Upper quantile paired with [`ENV_FLOOR_Q`] to measure a
108	/// probe's spread — how wide the bulk of the distribution sits
109	/// above its own floor.
110	const ENV_SPREAD_Q: f64 = 0.90;
111	
112	/// Census threshold for a micro-probe group, the batch census
113	/// rule ([`BATCH_OVER_MULT`]) rebased on the probe's scale: the
114	/// additive term is 5 ns rather than 50, because a per-pair
115	/// value is ~25 ns and a 50 ns floor would never be crossed.
116	const ENV_OVER_ADD_PS: u64 = 5_000;
117	
118	/// Batch buffer capacity in samples — the pipeline's memory
119	/// bound (512 KiB of u64 ps values). Fast benches fill it in
120	/// ~15–40 ms and flush full; slow benches flush earlier on
121	/// [`BATCH_TARGET_SECONDS`].
122	const BATCH_SAMPLES: usize = 65_536;
123	
124	/// Time-based batch flush (seconds): a partial batch flushes
125	/// once it spans this long, so slow benches still get a usable
126	/// time axis (drift/burst localization) from few samples.
127	const BATCH_TARGET_SECONDS: f64 = 0.05;
128	
129	/// Push-count mask between time checks in
130	/// [`BatchPipeline::push`] — one `Instant::now` per 1024
131	/// samples keeps the check cost off the per-sample path.
132	const BATCH_CHECK_MASK: usize = 1023;
133	
134	/// Quantile defining a batch's *robust* floor, the statistic the
135	/// gauge's drift/step signals read.
136	///
137	/// - The raw min is too sparse to grade movement: measured on a
138	///   quiet 3900X at inner=10 (100 ps lattice), adjacent batch
139	///   minima flipped between 22.0 and 23.0 ns — a 4.5% "step" on
140	///   a run with no state change, which alone would have graded
141	///   every quiet run F.
142	/// - The same batches' p10 sat on 23.0 ns run-wide and moved
143	///   only when the machine did. The left edge of the
144	///   distribution is sparse; a tenth of 65,536 samples is not.
145	const BATCH_FLOOR_Q: f64 = 0.10;
146	
147	/// Census threshold: a batch sample is "over floor" above
148	/// `max(BATCH_OVER_MULT x floor, floor + BATCH_OVER_ADD_PS)`,
149	/// applied per batch against the batch's own [`BATCH_FLOOR_Q`]
150	/// floor.
151	///
152	/// - Measured against the raw min instead, the census was
153	///   meaningless on any bench with a low tail: mpsc-2t batches
154	///   whose min landed on a 0.9 µs fast path (against a 6.5 µs
155	///   floor) counted 99.9% of their samples "over floor", and the
156	///   ones whose min landed normally counted 1%.
157	const BATCH_OVER_MULT: f64 = 1.5;
158	
159	/// Additive part of the census threshold (50 ns in ps).
160	const BATCH_OVER_ADD_PS: u64 = 50_000;
161	
162	/// Sleep-separated blocks: random sleep bounds (ms) between
163	/// blocks. Randomized so block boundaries don't phase-lock with
164	/// kernel ticks or workload periodicity; long enough to let the
165	/// scheduler / frequency state re-roll.
166	const BLOCK_SLEEP_MS_MIN: u64 = 1;
167	const BLOCK_SLEEP_MS_MAX: u64 = 10;
168	
169	/// Unrecorded post-wake warm-up per block (seconds). Each wake
170	/// pays a frequency ramp plus a cache refill, which must not leak
171	/// into the block's samples.
172	const BLOCK_WARMUP_SECONDS: f64 = 0.002;
173	
174	/// Histogram value bounds: 1 ps to 60 s at 3 sig figs. Values
175	/// are recorded in **picoseconds** — the timer reads integer ns,
176	/// but dividing a sample by `inner` in ps keeps the true sub-ns
177	/// per-call precision that ns recording truncated (a 4.7 ns call
178	/// no longer rounds to 5). The high bound is a sane-world
179	/// ceiling for one recorded sample, not a technical limit —
180	/// [`record_sample`] clamps above it and [`warn_invalid`] flags
181	/// the run.
182	const HIST_LOW_PS: u64 = 1;
183	const HIST_HIGH_PS: u64 = 60_000_000_000_000;
184	
185	/// Picoseconds per nanosecond: recorded values are ps, display
186	/// is ns.
187	const PS_PER_NS: f64 = 1000.0;
188	
189	/// Grade-block column widths, sized to each column's widest
190	/// realistic cell so right-aligned cells always leave the
191	/// two-space gap `qualify-environment`'s parser splits on.
192	///
193	/// - label columns (`grade`, `phase`) are left-aligned
194	/// - value columns are right-aligned; a signal that does not
195	///   apply to a row prints [`GB_BLANK`]
196	const GB_GRADE_W: usize = 5;
197	/// `phase` column: `warmup` is the widest phase.
198	const GB_PHASE_W: usize = 6;
199	/// `settle` column: `not settled` is the widest cell.
200	const GB_SETTLE_W: usize = 11;

341	///   detects frequency and state movement well and preemption
342	///   poorly; `interference` catches only the rare large
343	///   intrusion that lands inside a probe.

345	///   is a statement about the machine, which is actionable in a
346	///   way that an F on a blocking bench is not. Nothing warns yet.
347	#[derive(Debug)]
348	pub struct EnvGrade {
349	    /// Median over probes of each probe's spread: its upper
350	    /// quantile over its floor, relative.
351	    pub spread_frac: f64,
352	    /// Individual timer pairs above their probe's over-floor
353	    /// cut, as a fraction of all pairs in the series.
354	    pub interference_frac: f64,
355	    /// Floor movement from the first quarter of the probe series
356	    /// to the last, relative.
357	    pub drift_frac: f64,
358	    /// The largest floor shift any split of the series divides,
359	    /// relative.
360	    pub step_frac: f64,
361	    /// Where that split fell — seconds from warmup start.
362	    pub step_at_s: f64,
363	    /// Overall letter, worst signal wins: A, B, C, D, or F.
364	    pub letter: char,
365	}
366	
367	impl EnvGrade {
368	    /// Grade the environment from the warmup probe series; `None`
369	    /// when warmup produced no probes.
370	    pub fn from_probes(probes: &[ProbeSummary]) -> Option<Self> {
371	        if probes.is_empty() {
372	            return None;
373	        }
374	
375	        let spreads: Vec<f64> = probes
376	            .iter()
377	            .map(|p| {
378	                if p.floor_q_ps == 0 {
379	                    0.0
380	                } else {
381	                    (p.spread_q_ps as f64 - p.floor_q_ps as f64) / p.floor_q_ps as f64
382	                }
383	            })
384	            .collect();
385	        let spread_frac = median(&spreads).unwrap_or(0.0); // OK: `probes` is non-empty
386	
387	        let total: u64 = probes.iter().map(|p| p.pairs).sum();
388	        let over: u64 = probes.iter().map(|p| p.over_pairs).sum();
389	        let interference_frac = if total == 0 {
390	            0.0
391	        } else {
392	            over as f64 / total as f64
393	        };
394	
395	        let floors: Vec<f64> = probes.iter().map(|p| p.floor_q_ps as f64).collect();
396	        let n = floors.len();
397	        let quarter = (n / 4).max(1);
398	        let drift_frac = split_change(&floors[..quarter], &floors[n - quarter..]);
399	
400	        let times: Vec<f64> = probes.iter().map(|p| p.t_start_s).collect();
401	        let (step_frac, step_at_s) = best_split(&floors, &times);
402	
403	        let mut grade = Self {
404	            spread_frac,
405	            interference_frac,
406	            drift_frac,
407	            step_frac,
408	            step_at_s,
409	            letter: 'A',
410	        };
411	        grade.letter = score_letter(grade.scores().into_iter().fold(0, u8::max));
412	        Some(grade)
413	    }
414	
415	    /// Per-signal scores in print order: spread, interference,
416	    /// drift, step — each the count of its [`env_thresholds`]
417	    /// cutoffs crossed, composite is the worst.
418	    fn scores(&self) -> [u8; 4] {
419	        [
420	            score(self.spread_frac, env_thresholds::SPREAD),
421	            score(self.interference_frac, env_thresholds::INTERFERENCE),
422	            score(self.drift_frac, env_thresholds::DRIFT),
423	            score(self.step_frac, env_thresholds::STEP),
424	        ]
425	    }
426	
427	    /// Letters for the gauge line's printed signals, in print
428	    /// order — all four composite inputs, so the worst letter on
429	    /// the line *is* the composite.
430	    pub fn signal_letters(&self) -> [char; 4] {
431	        self.scores().map(score_letter)
432	    }
433	}

435	/// How far a probe's floor may sit from the settled level and
436	/// still count as settled: [`settle`]'s band.
437	///
438	/// - One percent, the same number as [`env_thresholds::DRIFT`]'s
439	///   A cutoff: "settled" means the movement left is movement the
440	///   environment grade would have called A.
441	pub const SETTLE_TOL: f64 = 0.01;
442	
443	/// When the warmup stretch settled: seconds from warmup start to
444	/// the first probe from which the floor stayed inside
445	/// [`SETTLE_TOL`] of the level warmup ended at. `None` when there
446	/// is nothing to measure (an empty stretch or a zero floor).
447	///
448	/// - **Why report it at all.** Once warmup deliberately spans the
449	///   ramp, the grade stops seeing the ramp, which is warmup
450	///   working, and would otherwise leave the report saying nothing
451	///   about a box that took a second to come up to speed. The
452	///   letter answers "was it settled when measurement started";
453	///   this answers "how long did that take", which is the number
454	///   the "Dynamic warmup" Todo turns into a stopping rule.
455	/// - The settled level is the *tail window's* median floor
456	///   (`tail`), so it is the same reference the warmup grade is
457	///   scored against.
458	/// - The rule is "when did the floor last leave the band": the
459	///   settle time is the probe after the last one outside it, so
460	///   movement anywhere in the stretch is reflected, not just
461	///   movement a suffix median survives. A suffix-median rule was
462	///   tried first and read `settled 0.00s` on stretches whose own
463	///   `drift` signal graded F: a minority of moved probes never
464	///   shifts the median.
465	/// - "Outside the band" is asked of a [`SETTLE_WINDOW`]-probe
466	///   *median*, not of a probe. The letter is computed from
467	///   medians, so a per-probe rule disagrees with it: on a
468	///   bimodally-flickering 3900X floor, single probes leave a 1%
469	///   band constantly while every median the grade takes stays
470	///   put, and settle time read "never settled" beside a
471	///   drift/step of 0.00% A. A window median makes the two
472	///   answer the same question: a state the box actually held
473	///   for a while.
474	/// - **The state has to have held through the graded tail
475	///   window.** An excursion inside that window reports
476	///   [`Settle::Never`], never a time. Without this the statistic
477	///   tracks the *budget* instead of the box: settle is the last
478	///   excursion's end, and a box that keeps flickering has its
479	///   last excursion near the end of warmup whenever warmup ends.
480	///   Measured 2026-07-30 on the 3900X: `--settle-time 1.5`
481	///   reported a 1.0 s median settle and `--settle-time 5` a
482	///   4.63 s one, on the same box in the same state. The tail
483	///   window is the right span to demand because it is the one the
484	///   letter is scored over: "settled" now means the stretch the
485	///   grade looked at contained no movement at all.
486	/// - It follows that a stretch still moving at its very end is
487	///   also [`Settle::Never`], rather than reporting its last
488	///   probe's time, which would read as "settled, just barely".
489	pub fn settle(warm: &[ProbeSummary], tail: &[ProbeSummary]) -> Option<Settle> {
490	    let tail_floors: Vec<f64> = tail.iter().map(|p| p.floor_q_ps as f64).collect();
491	    let level = median(&tail_floors)?;
492	    if level <= 0.0 {
493	        return None;
494	    }
495	    let windows = window_floors(warm);
496	    let last_out = windows
497	        .iter()
498	        .rposition(|&f| (f - level).abs() / level > SETTLE_TOL);
499	    // The graded window's start: settling later than this means
500	    // the box moved inside the stretch the letter was scored over.
501	    let held_from = tail.first().map_or(f64::INFINITY, |p| p.t_start_s);
502	    match last_out {
503	        // The probe after the last excursion, when one follows it
504	        // and the state then held through the graded window.
505	        Some(i) => match warm.get(i + 1) {
506	            Some(p) if p.t_start_s <= held_from => Some(Settle::At(p.t_start_s)),
507	            _ => Some(Settle::Never),
508	        },
509	        None => warm.first().map(|p| Settle::At(p.t_start_s)),
510	    }
511	}
512

514	/// band, or that it never did.
515	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
516	pub enum Settle {
517	    /// Seconds from warmup start to the settled floor.
518	    At(f64),
519	    /// Still moving when the stretch ended: the box needs more
520	    /// warming than it was given (`--settle-time`).
521	    Never,
522	}

526	    /// on the warmup row, parsed back by `qualify-environment`.
527	    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
528	        match self {
529	            Settle::At(s) => write!(f, "{s:.2}s"),
530	            Settle::Never => write!(f, "not settled"),
531	        }
532	    }
533	}

536	/// floor has to hold to count as a state the box was in, rather

545	///   the same stretch's `drift` (a quarter against a quarter)
546	///   graded F. The two now summarize over comparable spans at
547	///   any series length.
548	const SETTLE_WINDOW: usize = 8;
549	
550	/// Running forward-window median of probe floors: index `i` is
551	/// the median of the next [`SETTLE_WINDOW`] floors from `i`.
552	///
553	/// - The window is [`SETTLE_WINDOW`] probes, or a quarter of a
554	///   series too short for that, the span `drift` compares.
555	/// - The trailing windows are the same length: the last
556	///   `w - 1` positions have fewer probes ahead of
557	///   them, so the window is anchored at the end instead of

were an artifact of this tool: calibration spun ~1 s on core 0
before every invocation, which carried the box past a transition
it would otherwise meet mid-measurement. Deleting calibration
removes that accidental pre-warm, which is what the rung
predicted. So far so expected.

`interference` reads 0.00% and `spread` 0.48%, and sampling

  0.80s        4980 MHz

holds there for ~0.75 s of sustained load, then steps to 99.7%.

grades reads A, `drift` and `step` at 0.00%. The F is the step
landing inside the window, nothing else.

trailing probes to answer "did it end settled", and it answered
yes while the box sat at 4841 MHz. A dwell *is* steady, so a

614	### The clock as a warmup criterion (design, unmeasured)
615	
616	The obvious use is the warmup exit condition, and it solves a
617	problem no timing-based criterion can. A steadiness test
618	cannot distinguish "settled at the top" from "dwelling at an
619	intermediate P-state", because a dwell is *steady*. A clock
620	reading distinguishes them directly.
621	
622	We think the right gate is **clock stability under load**, not
623	a fraction of max:
624	
625	- A threshold on `cpuinfo_max_freq` would need tuning between
626	  the two boxes' sustained fractions (96.1% on the 3900X,
627	  99.7% on the 7600x) against their pre-load readings, and a
628	  thermally-limited laptop would plateau lower still and never
629	  reach it — while that plateau *is* its honest sustained
630	  clock.
631	- Stability under load needs no tuned constant. Warmup is
632	  itself sustained load, so the climb happens during warmup if
633	  warmup lasts long enough; the ~200 ms measured here is the
634	  scale.
635	- Report the ratio for information; do not grade on it. The
636	  letter should stay a statement about measured time, with the
637	  clock explaining it.
638	
639	Portability caveat: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is amd-pstate-specific,
640	and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq` returns the requested
641	rather than the delivered frequency. Any use must be optional
642	— read it where present, fall back to timing-only otherwise.
643	An Intel laptop is the next box to check, and the interesting
644	one: a thermally-limited machine should show the opposite
645	shape, starting fast and decaying under sustained load, which
646	is the direction neither desktop can produce.
647	
648	### Grading the box without the bench
649	
650	The run grade describes the run it printed, and a run's
651	steadiness is largely its workload's character. That is the
652	right answer for a histogram's caption and the wrong one for
653	the question "is this machine fit to measure on" — the
654	question the retired `calibrate` grade was really answering,
655	and the one -7 removes an answer to.
656	
657	Warmup is the only window a run has where no workload has
658	entered the numbers yet, so that is where the environment
659	certificate is measured. The probe times timer pairs and
660	nothing else, which is what makes the resulting letter a
661	statement about the machine.
662	
663	Signals against the run grade's four:
664	
665	- `interference`, `drift`, `step` — the same questions with
666	  the same definitions, over a different population. `drift`
667	  is the one the cycle needs most: it is the frequency-ramp
668	  detector the 7600x F diagnosis and the 3900X bistability
669	  both call for.
670	- `spread` — new here: how wide a probe's bulk sits above its
671	  own floor. There is no run-side analog worth having,
672	  because a bench's spread is mostly its workload (park /
673	  unpark bimodality is a fact about `mpsc`, not the box)
674	  while a timer pair has no character of its own.
675	- `bursts` — dropped. The contamination it would count is
676	  already counted by `interference`, and a hot-probe fraction
677	  adds nothing a spread and a census do not already say.
678	
679	Thresholds are separate from the run grade's even where the
680	numbers currently match, because the two grade different
681	populations and should be free to diverge as measurement
682	says they should — as `interference`'s since have (see
683	[What the probe cannot see](#what-the-probe-cannot-see)).
684	
685	One caveat on "without the bench", added once probes moved to
686	the seams: the *warmup* stretch is measured with nothing but
687	warmup steps behind it, but a seam probe shares the box with
688	the bench — on a 2t bench, with its still-spinning worker.
689	That is a truer picture of the environment the run actually
690	had and a slightly less pure measure of the machine alone.
691	The warmup stretch remains the clean one.

  99.7% on the 7600x) against their pre-load readings, and a
  thermally-limited laptop would plateau lower still and never
  reach it — while that plateau *is* its honest sustained
  clock.
- Stability under load needs no tuned constant. Warmup is
  itself sustained load, so the climb happens during warmup if
  warmup lasts long enough; the ~200 ms measured here is the
  scale.
- Report the ratio for information; do not grade on it. The
  letter should stay a statement about measured time, with the
  clock explaining it.

Portability caveat: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is amd-pstate-specific,
and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq` returns the requested
rather than the delivered frequency. Any use must be optional
— read it where present, fall back to timing-only otherwise.
An Intel laptop is the next box to check, and the interesting
one: a thermally-limited machine should show the opposite
shape, starting fast and decaying under sustained load, which
is the direction neither desktop can produce.

### Grading the box without the bench

The run grade describes the run it printed, and a run's
steadiness is largely its workload's character. That is the
right answer for a histogram's caption and the wrong one for
the question "is this machine fit to measure on" — the
question the retired `calibrate` grade was really answering,
and the one -7 removes an answer to.

Warmup is the only window a run has where no workload has
entered the numbers yet, so that is where the environment
certificate is measured. The probe times timer pairs and
nothing else, which is what makes the resulting letter a
statement about the machine.

Signals against the run grade's four:

- `interference`, `drift`, `step` — the same questions with
  the same definitions, over a different population. `drift`
  is the one the cycle needs most: it is the frequency-ramp
  detector the 7600x F diagnosis and the 3900X bistability
  both call for.
- `spread` — new here: how wide a probe's bulk sits above its
  own floor. There is no run-side analog worth having,
  because a bench's spread is mostly its workload (park /
  unpark bimodality is a fact about `mpsc`, not the box)
  while a timer pair has no character of its own.
- `bursts` — dropped. The contamination it would count is
  already counted by `interference`, and a hot-probe fraction
  adds nothing a spread and a census do not already say.

Thresholds are separate from the run grade's even where the
numbers currently match, because the two grade different
populations and should be free to diverge as measurement
says they should — as `interference`'s since have (see
[What the probe cannot see](#what-the-probe-cannot-see)).

One caveat on "without the bench", added once probes moved to
the seams: the *warmup* stretch is measured with nothing but
warmup steps behind it, but a seam probe shares the box with
the bench — on a 2t bench, with its still-spinning worker.
That is a truer picture of the environment the run actually
had and a slightly less pure measure of the machine alone.
The warmup stretch remains the clean one.

The 0.23.5 single-commit cycle, banking two design decisions

  mentions across TODO.md, src/harness.rs, src/gauge.rs,

  loop.** The harness has three warms (per-run
  `warmup_and_probe`, once-per-process `process_warm`,

  one probe series, prober and time origin, and the entry now
  commits to all three becoming exit-condition policies over a
  single mechanism rather than growing a fourth variant

  pinning experiment made placement the dominant factor (4-18x)

  design: cooperative knowledge (the `--pin` pool) layered over
  observational knowledge (a `/proc/self/task/` sweep at batch
  seams, children recursively; CPU-time deltas identify active
  threads with no bench cooperation). Sampled truth at the step
  detector's own granularity, so batches get placement-class
  labels (attributed steps) and unpinned `--blocks` runs

235	### The warm pin's remaining job
236	
237	Pinning main before the tick-rate read is what survives of the
238	calibration pin, and it is now close to ceremony. Measured on the
239	3900X, the read is insensitive to placement: 3.792891 ticks/ns
240	pinned to CPU0 against 3.792888 on CPU11 and CPU23, an ~8e-7
241	spread. It is a ratio of TSC ticks to monotonic nanoseconds over
242	~10 ms, so an interruption inflates both sides and cancels, and
243	`constant_tsc`/`nonstop_tsc` mean there is no per-core rate to
244	discover.
245	
246	That matters because CPU0 is measurably the kernel's busiest
247	core here, taking 4-10x the `LOC`, `CAL`, `RES` and `TLB` counts
248	of CPU11 or CPU23 with no `irqbalance` running. Pinning a
249	measurement there would be a poor default; pinning a
250	cancellation-immune ratio there is merely pointless. The pin and
251	`--no-pin-cal` stay for now because the "Dynamic warmup"
252	Todo turns warmup into a real timing phase that will want a pin
253	back, and the placement question is recorded there rather than
254	churned twice.

### The warm pin's remaining job

Pinning main before the tick-rate read is what survives of the
calibration pin, and it is now close to ceremony. Measured on the
3900X, the read is insensitive to placement: 3.792891 ticks/ns
pinned to CPU0 against 3.792888 on CPU11 and CPU23, an ~8e-7
spread. It is a ratio of TSC ticks to monotonic nanoseconds over
~10 ms, so an interruption inflates both sides and cancels, and
`constant_tsc`/`nonstop_tsc` mean there is no per-core rate to
discover.

That matters because CPU0 is measurably the kernel's busiest
core here, taking 4-10x the `LOC`, `CAL`, `RES` and `TLB` counts
of CPU11 or CPU23 with no `irqbalance` running. Pinning a
measurement there would be a poor default; pinning a
cancellation-immune ratio there is merely pointless. The pin and
`--no-pin-cal` stay for now because the "Dynamic warmup"
Todo turns warmup into a real timing phase that will want a pin
back, and the placement question is recorded there rather than
churned twice.

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`): the cycle's
18	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
19	  it and starts at `-1`; see
20	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
21	  cycle:
22	  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
23	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
24	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
25	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
26	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
27	    statement + plan ladder).
28	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...): the
30	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
31	  needs; each runs through the
32	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
33	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`): the cycle's
34	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
35	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
36	    `## Done`.
37	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
38	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
39	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
40	    changed.
41	
42	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
43	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
44	result must always be published at close-out. See
45	[Pushing](#pushing).
46	
47	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
48	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides: `X.Y.Z-3.0`
49	Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
50	Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
51	at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
52	suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
53	for the local-ladder mechanics.
54	
55	## Chores sections
56	
57	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
58	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
59	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
60	should have a reference to it on a rung of its section's
61	as-built ladder in a chores file.
62	
63	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
64	`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
65	with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`).
66	**Each work commit then appends its own as-built rung
67	(`- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, literal `[[N]]` placeholder)
68	+ narrative note as it lands**: the chores record is built
69	up per commit, not held back and written all at once at
70	close-out; close-out only *finalizes* (title sync, design
71	subsections, retiring the `## In Progress` block). A
72	single-commit cycle's ladder is one bare-`X.Y.Z` rung. The
73	rung placeholders are backfilled later, once the commit is
74	permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
75	
76	Opening a section also appends its title-only
77	`- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
78	`## Table of Contents`, synced to the final title at
79	close-out.
80	
81	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
82	design subsection pattern, rung / reference formatting)
83	live in
84	[agent-data/notes.md](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions).
85	
86	### Commits backfill
87	
88	An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA, but a SHA
89	isn't stable until the commit lands on a **permanent
90	branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch branch that
91	won't be rewritten); a rebase or squash rewrites it on the
92	way. So:
93	
94	- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]`
95	  placeholder**.
96	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
97	  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
98	  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
99	  push later: **each push backfills the rungs of the
100	  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
101	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands,
102	  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
103	  invalidate.
104	
105	Backfill replaces the placeholder with a file-local `[[N]]`
106	ref, defined as the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's
107	`# References` (format in agent-data/notes.md
108	[Chores commit references](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
109	Sections predating the ladder form keep their legacy
110	`Commits:` lines; backfill those where they exist. A
111	section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
112	deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
113	`git log --grep "<title>"`.
114	
115	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma: a
116	**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
117	close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
118	SHA must be permanent.
119	
120	## Preparation
121	
122	The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
123	setup (a lightweight cycle omits it; see
124	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):
125	
126	- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
127	  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
128	  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
129	  project-specific; see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
130	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
131	  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
132	  - A **bold title line**, which will be the chores
133	    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
134	  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
135	  - A **plan ladder**.
136	- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)**:
137	  append a `##` header with the title it records, the
138	  cycle's anticipated close-out title.
139	
140	## Work-N
141	
142	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
143	implement the change. As many as needed:
144	
145	- Each commit runs through the
146	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
147	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
148	  visibility).
149	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
150	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
151	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
152	  scope grows enough (see
153	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
154	
155	## Close-out
156	
157	The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
158	only, and the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
159	what happens post-squash:
160	
161	- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
162	  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
163	- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
164	  and grown per commit; see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
165	  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
166	    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
167	    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
168	    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
169	  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
170	    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
171	  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
172	    notes.
173	  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
174	    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
175	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
176	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
177	
178	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
179	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time;
180	see [Pushing](#pushing).
181	
182	## Numbering
183	
184	Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix: `-0`
185	Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/... Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
186	recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme (disambiguation,
187	nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
188	format, and the per-phase bump) lives in
189	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
190	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
191	
192	## Per-commit flow
193	
194	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
195	through:
196	
197	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
198	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
199	   root).
200	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
201	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
202	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
203	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
204	4. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
205	   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
206	   example the cargo cycle is:
207	   1. `cargo fmt`
208	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
209	   3. `cargo test`
210	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
211	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
212	5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
213	   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
214	   changes and we iterate until complete.
215	6. **Write the commit description**; see
216	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
217	7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
218	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
219	8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R .` for
220	   the work repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last
221	   keeps the verb visible):
222	
223	   ```
224	   jj commit -m \
225	   "<type>: <short description>" \
226	   -m "<intro paragraph>
227	
228	   - file1: gist
229	   - file2: gist
230	
231	   ochid: /.claude/<chid>" \
232	   -R .
233	   ```
234	
235	**Two overrides apply:**
236	
237	- **Deviation or question**: any time the work deviates
238	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
239	  surface it; don't push through.
240	- **ESC-ESC**: the user can interrupt at any point to pull
241	  a review or question forward.
242	
243	## Commit description
244	
245	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
246	
247	```
248	<type>: <short description>
249	```
250	
251	Titles carry **no trailing `(<version>)` suffix**. The
252	version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
253	[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming
254	you're running the version you're testing, not a per-commit
255	title marker. We think per-commit version-in-title is
256	unstable on large projects: many changes are in flight
257	simultaneously, and a
258	version is only stable once merged into the main repo, so
259	titles don't carry one.
260	
261	### Title
262	
263	- ≤50 chars total.
264	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
265	  `docs`, `chore`.
266	- Favor terse phrasings.
267	- **Distinct per step**: each of a cycle's commits gets its
268	  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
269	  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
270	  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the
271	  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
272	  AGENTS.md
273	  [Conventional-commit shape](../AGENTS.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
274	
275	### Body
276	
277	[Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),
278	wrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:
279	
280	- **Work-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file
281	  changed (file plus a one-line gist). Sub-bullets for
282	  files with multiple distinct changes:
283	
284	  ```
285	  - path/to/file1
286	    - first distinct change
287	    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line
288	       with continuation indented 5
289	  ```
290	
291	  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the
292	  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the
293	  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any
294	  "why" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.
295	
296	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe
297	  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.
298	
299	### Trailer
300	
301	`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
302	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](../AGENTS.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
303	in AGENTS.md for the convention.
304	
305	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
306	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
307	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
308	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
309	
310	## Reviewing changes
311	
312	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
313	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
314	editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:
315	
316	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
317	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
318	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
319	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
320	
321	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
322	it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
323	`jj show -r @-`.
324	
325	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
326	close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
327	are in [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets).
328	
329	## Pushing
330	
331	### Policy
332	
333	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
334	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
335	the cycle's result must be published.
336	
337	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
338	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
339	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
340	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
341	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
342	the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
343	
344	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
345	the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
346	commit-description review (show title+body and stop), and the
347	hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
348	default*.
349	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
350	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
351	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
352	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
353	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
354	
355	- **Explicit grant**: never inferred from a task merely being
356	  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
357	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
358	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
359	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
360	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
361	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
362	  unattended") waives them.
363	- **Bounded goal**: covers the named task only; does not carry
364	  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
365	- **Destructive ops still pause**: delegation covers the task's
366	  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
367	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
368	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
369	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
370	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
371	  reaches this.
372	- **Still transparent**: report each commit/push as it lands
373	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
374	- **When in doubt, ask**: ambiguous authorization falls back to
375	  per-push approval.
376	
377	### Shape at close-out push
378	
379	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
380	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
381	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
382	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
383	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
384	
385	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
386	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
387	  focused on one or two files.
388	- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)*: `main` gains a
389	  merge commit (`X.Y.Z`); cycle commits stay reachable via
390	  two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal
391	  shape. See [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe)
392	  for the full setup sequence.
393	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
394	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
395	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
396	  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.
397	
398	Set up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use
399	`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.
400	
401	### Merge non-ff recipe
402	
403	Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
404	close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
405	close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
406	(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
407	Work commit:
408	
409	1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge**: `jj rebase -r
410	   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
411	   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
412	   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
413	   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.
414	
415	   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
416	   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
417	2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
418	   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
419	   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
420	   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
421	3. **Push**: `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
422	
423	**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
424	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
425	immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
426	push force-updates `main`.
427	The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
428	the close-out push.
429	
430	**Viewing the result (not a push step).** After merge
431	non-ff close-outs land, read the history with
432	`jj log -r ..@ -n <N>`: the graph renders each cycle as its
433	trapezoid, with close-out titles down the trunk's left edge and
434	the cycle's Work rungs indented on the side leg, so trunk and
435	internals are both visible at once. For git-side tooling
436	(which lists commits flat instead of drawing the graph),
437	`git log --first-parent` recovers the trunk view: one
438	close-out merge per cycle, rungs skipped; plain `git log`
439	interleaves every cycle's rungs into one long list.
440	
441	### vc-x1 push wrapper
442	
443	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
444	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
445	work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
446	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
447	
448	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
449	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
450	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
451	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`;
452	this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
453	
454	### .claude cadence
455	
456	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
457	with every work-repo commit in that push.
458	
459	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
460	across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
461	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
462	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
463	
464	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
465	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
466	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
467	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
468	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
469	
470	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
471	session information created, which we don't worry about.
472	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
473	remain empty.
474	
475	### Bot communication at the reviews
476	
477	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
478	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
479	
480	- **At Work review**: summarize what changed and stop.
481	  "Work complete. Please review."
482	- **At Commit Description review**: present `$TITLE`
483	  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
484	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
485	  --body ...` invocation by default.
486	- **At Post close-out review**: surface the shape
487	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
488	  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
489	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
490	
491	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
492	
493	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
494	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
495	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
496	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
497	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
498	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
499	
500	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
501	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
502	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
503	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
504	  turn's *final* push.
505	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
506	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
507	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
508	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
509	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
510	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
511	  user, after the turn, can capture it
512	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
513	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
514	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
515	  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
516	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
517	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
518	  closing line after the push; that is a known slip.
519	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
520	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
521	  quiet. It flushes all bot session information into the
522	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
523	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
524	
525	### Recovery
526	
527	- **If push exits before its last stage**, meaning `push-work`
528	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish didn't run
529	  (`squash-push-bot` in `vc-x1 push --status` / `--from`
530	  stage names), run the squash+push by hand:
531	
532	  ```
533	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
534	  ```
535	
536	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
537	  exit, with no log file to chase.
538	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
539	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
540	  agents).
541	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
542	    command runs: the invocation's own record plus any
543	    closing response land after the squash.
544	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
545	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
546	    change; it is not under the user's control.)
547	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
548	    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
549	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
550	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
551	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
552	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
553	- **Clear push's saved state** after any out-of-band
554	  recovery, via `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml` or `vc-x1 push
555	  <bookmark> --restart`; otherwise push resumes from a
556	  stale stage.
557	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
558	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
559	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
560	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
561	  push.
562	- **`vc-x1 push` after a manual merge setup published an
563	  empty commit** (seen at the 0.22.0 close-out). `vc-x1
564	  push` *creates* the work commit itself from pending
565	  changes + `--title`/`--body`; it does not publish an
566	  already-committed shape. Invoked after the
567	  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) (work repo
568	  clean, merge in place), it minted an **empty** commit on
569	  the old `main` tip, stamped the ochid on it, and pushed
570	  that, leaving the merge unreferenced and `main` without
571	  the cycle's content. Prevention: after a manual shape
572	  setup, push with `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`
573	  directly (the recipe's step 3), never `vc-x1 push`.
574	  Recovery, in order (nothing is lost, the merge still
575	  exists):
576	  1. `jj describe <merge>` to append the
577	     `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>` trailer the stray got
578	     instead (rewrites the merge's commit id; its chid,
579	     what the bot side references, is stable).
580	  2. `jj abandon <stray> --ignore-immutable`.
581	  3. `jj bookmark set main -r <merge> --allow-backwards`,
582	     `jj new <merge>`, then `jj git push --bookmark main
583	     -R .` (remote rewrite, needs approval).
584	  4. Bot repo: `jj describe <bot-commit> --ignore-immutable
585	     -R .claude` to point its `ochid:` at the merge's chid,
586	     then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .claude`
587	     (restores the `main == main@origin` preflight
588	     invariant).
589	
590	  The recovered shape, `jj log -r ..@` (0.22.0, elided):
591	
592	  ```
593	  @  smpozlop ... (empty) (no description set)
594	  ◆    yzvlvtku ... main d9bb5882
595	  ├─╮  fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise
596	  │ ◆  ztxvxuru ... fix-calibration f4b155a8
597	  │ │  feat: always-on calibration self-checks
598	  │ ~  (three more rungs)
599	  │ ◆  tskxkxsk ... 6d5784de
600	  ├─╯  fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
601	  ◆  sktyvwrq ... f006b09e
602	  │  feat: amortized + cached calibration
603	  ```
604	
605	## Iterative work
606	
607	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
608	from incremental review, loop:
609	
610	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
611	2. Make the next round of changes.
612	3. User reviews the round (see
613	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
614	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
615	   new empty `@`.
616	5. If not done, go to step 2.
617	
618	Same jj mechanics as a
619	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
620	single-commit scope, so the version
621	doesn't change.
622	
623	## Sub-cycle ladders
624	
625	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
626	[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
627	commits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and
628	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
629	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch,
630	for review and bisection only.
631	
632	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
633	
634	For each Work commit in the ladder:
635	
636	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
637	2. Do the commit's work.
638	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
639	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**: for code, build and clippy
640	   alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the full
641	   suite, raising bisection cost.
642	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
643	   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
644	   into one final commit.
645	
646	### Navigating the ladder
647	
648	Common moves:
649	
650	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
651	  from its base.
652	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
653	  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
654	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
655	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
656	  isolation.
657	
658	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
659	descendants auto-rebase.
660	
661	### Close-out: squash the ladder
662	
663	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
664	
665	```
666	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
667	```
668	
669	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
670	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
671	After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
672	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
673	
674	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.
675	
676	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
677	when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.
678	
679	### Recovery
680	
681	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
682	prior commits:
683	
684	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
685	  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
686	  parent.
687	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
688	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
689	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
690	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
691	  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
692	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
693	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
694	
695	# References
696	
697	- [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets): revset primitives
698	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
699	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
700	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
701	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
702	  bisection cost.
703
